name: Rubell Museum
overview: A contemporary art museum in the Allapattah neighbourhood of Miami, in six connected former industrial warehouses converted by Selldorf Architects, with 36 galleries on one level (museum website).

Don and Mera Rubell opened it in 1993 in Wynwood as the Rubell Family Collection/Contemporary Arts Foundation; it moved to Allapattah in December 2019 under its present name, and a second site opened in Washington, DC, in October 2022 (museum website).

The collection holds over 7,700 works by more than 1,000 artists, among them Jean-Michel Basquiat, Keith Haring, Jeff Koons, Cindy Sherman, Yayoi Kusama, Kara Walker, Purvis Young and Mickalene Thomas, bought by the family since 1965; the museum has drawn over 50 exhibitions from it, including 30 Americans (2008) (museum website).
funding_verdict: Rubell Museum: founded and run by the Rubell family; tickets, memberships and donations are asked for, amounts not published on the pages read

name: Montgomery Museum of Fine Arts
aliases: Montgomery Museum of Fine Arts Association
overview: The Montgomery Museum of Fine Arts is at One Museum Drive in Blount Cultural Park, Montgomery, Alabama, in a 43,000 square foot building that also holds ArtWorks, the Wilson Auditorium and the Hobbes Library (museum website, history page).

It was founded in 1930 by the artist John Kelly Fitzpatrick, Mrs. Harry S. Houghton and the Morning View Painters, and began in an abandoned school building the City of Montgomery provided at one dollar a year; it occupied 440 South McDonough Street from 1959 to 1988 and opened in Blount Cultural Park in 1988 (museum website, history page).

What is there: the history page gives no total object count. It gives subsets: the Weil Collection of 500 Old Master prints, 52 pieces of studio art glass, nearly 100 pieces of First Period Worcester porcelain from the Loeb donation (as of 2007) and 100 Yousuf Karsh photographs. Named works include Mary Cassatt's Francoise in Green, Sewing, Thomas Hart Benton's Ozark Autumn and Edmonia Lewis's Hiawatha's Marriage, with African art and works by Alabama African American artists acquired in 2019 (museum website, history page).
funding_verdict: Montgomery Museum of Fine Arts: mainly private gifts and endowment, with a small earned income

name: New Britain Museum of American Art
aliases: New Britain Museum of American Art Inc
overview: An art museum at 56 Lexington Street, New Britain, Connecticut (museum website).

The museum traces its roots to the New Britain Institute, established in 1853; it began acquiring American art in 1894, John Butler Talcott started an acquisition fund in 1903 and Sanford Low became its first director in 1937 (museum website).

What is there: about 9,000 paintings, works on paper, sculptures and photographs of American art, including the Sanford B. D. Low Illustration Collection with works by Norman Rockwell (museum website).
funding_verdict: New Britain Museum of American Art: private, from donors, named acquisition funds and investment income

name: Flux Factory
overview: Artist-led non-profit arts space in Long Island City, Queens, at 39-31 29th Street (Flux Factory history page), with a second venue, Flux IV, at 56-21 2nd Street (Flux Factory).

Began in 1994 when seven artists rented a former spice factory on the Williamsburg waterfront in Brooklyn. It became a 501(c)(3) in 1999 (Flux Factory history page). ProPublica lists its tax exemption as issued in November 1999.

It was priced out of Williamsburg in 2002 and displaced by eminent domain in 2009 (Flux Factory history page). It has rented a converted greeting card factory in Long Island City since 2009 (Hyperallergic, Valentina Di Liscia, 17 November 2021).
funding_verdict: Flux Factory: public and philanthropic grants: New York City Department of Cultural Affairs, New York State Council on the Arts and the Andy Warhol Foundation

name: Museum of the City of New York
aliases: Museum of the City of New York, Inc.
overview: A museum of New York City's history at 1220 Fifth Avenue between 103rd and 104th Streets, in a Georgian Colonial-Revival building by Joseph H. Freedlander, built from 1929 to 1932 (museum website).
Henry Collins Brown, a Scottish-born writer, founded it in 1923; it was first housed in Gracie Mansion (museum website).

What is there: about 750,000 objects, including prints, photographs, decorative arts, costumes, paintings, sculpture, toys and theatrical memorabilia. Named holdings are Eugene O'Neill's handwritten manuscripts, a complete room of Duncan Phyfe furniture, 412 glass negatives by Jacob Riis, a suit worn to George Washington's Inaugural Ball and the Carrie Walter Stettheimer dollhouse, which contains a miniature work by Marcel Duchamp. The collections were acquired through purchases and contributions (museum website; audited financial statements 2025).
funding_verdict: Museum of the City of New York: mixed, gifts, events, endowment income and a city operating grant

name: Park Avenue Armory
aliases: Thompson Arts Center at Park Avenue Armory
overview: A nonprofit arts venue in a landmarked armory in New York, built from 1877 to 1881 by the Seventh Regiment of the National Guard, whose main space is the 55,000-square-foot Wade Thompson Drill Hall (Antiques and The Arts Weekly, 10 July 2015; NYC Department of Cultural Affairs).

Run by the Seventh Regiment Armory Conservancy under founding president Rebecca Robertson; its first production was in September 2007 (ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer; NYC Department of Cultural Affairs).

The building holds 18 period rooms by designers such as Louis Comfort Tiffany and Stanford White (Antiques and The Arts Weekly, 10 July 2015); the World Monuments Fund listed it in 2000 among the '100 Most Endangered Historic Sites in the World' (NYC Department of Cultural Affairs).
funding_verdict: Park Avenue Armory: one family's money above all, plus tickets, rentals and some public capital

name: Smack Mellon
overview: Nonprofit arts organisation at 92 Plymouth Street in DUMBO, Brooklyn, across from Brooklyn Bridge Park, that aims to "nurture and support emerging, under-recognized mid-career, and women artists" through exhibitions, studio space and technical help (Smack Mellon).
Founded in 1995 by the artist Andrea Reynosa and the musician Kevin Vertrees in their loft at 135 Plymouth Street. Reynosa was the founding executive director (Wikipedia; Smack Mellon).
From 1996 to 2004 it showed work in several DUMBO spaces donated by the Walentas family and Two Trees Management (Smack Mellon).
funding_verdict: Smack Mellon: mixed public and private: city and state arts agencies, foundations and individual donors

name: Allen Memorial Art Museum
overview: The Allen Memorial Art Museum is at 87 North Main Street, Oberlin, Ohio, on the campus of Oberlin College (museum website).
It was founded in 1917 to support teaching at Oberlin College, and admission has always been free (museum website, overview page).

What is there: a searchable database of more than 15,000 works; the collection is particularly strong in 17th century Dutch and Flemish painting, Japanese prints, early modern art and African art. A Japanese print, The Courtesan Somenosuke of the Matsubaya House by Chonunsai Eishi, came through the Mary A. Ainsworth Bequest in 1950 (museum website, collections page).
funding_verdict: Allen Memorial Art Museum: a college museum; the pages read name no funders

name: Rhode Island School of Design Museum (RISD Museum)
aliases: Museum of Art, Rhode Island School of Design
overview: An art and design museum at 20 North Main Street, Providence, Rhode Island, attached to the Rhode Island School of Design (museum website).
The museum states it was established in 1877 (museum website, Who We Are).

What is there: more than 100,000 works of art and design, of which 1,938 are on view, 85,862 are online and 2,528 are recent acquisitions; paintings, sculpture, decorative arts, costume and textiles and furniture from antiquity to the present (museum website, Who We Are).
funding_verdict: RISD Museum: part of a private art school, funded through the school's tuition-led budget plus donors and named acquisition funds

name: Taubman Museum of Art
overview: The Taubman Museum of Art is at 110 Salem Avenue SE in downtown Roanoke, Virginia, and opened there on 8 November 2008 (WVTF, 6 March 2026).

It began as the Roanoke Fine Arts Center in the 1950s, moved to the Cherry Hill estate in 1965, became the Roanoke Museum of Fine Arts in 1980, moved to Center in the Square in 1983 and was renamed the Art Museum of Western Virginia in 1992; in 2005 its board announced the new building would be named for Ambassador Nicholas Taubman and Eugenia Taubman for their lead gift (WVTF, 6 March 2026).

What is there: more than 2,500 works focused on American art from the 19th century to today, with 241 newly acquired works shown for the 75th anniversary. The Horace G. Fralin Charitable Trust began acquiring works by major American artists in the 1990s, and in 2002 Peggy Macdowell Thomas gave her entire Eakins Collection (WVTF, 6 March 2026).
funding_verdict: Taubman Museum of Art: private gifts and earned income, with an endowment-scale balance sheet

name: Memorial Art Gallery of the University of Rochester
aliases: University of Rochester Memorial Art Gallery
overview: An art museum at 500 University Avenue, Rochester, New York, the Memorial Art Gallery of the University of Rochester (museum website).
Emily Sibley Watson gave the gallery to the community in 1913; it was free to the public for its first 56 years (University of Rochester, May 2026).
What is there: a permanent collection of more than 13,000 objects spanning ancient to contemporary art (museum website; University of Rochester).
funding_verdict: Memorial Art Gallery: university-owned, funded by members, the university, a state arts council and a campaign for free admission

name: Crocker Art Museum
overview: Crocker Art Museum, 216 O Street, Sacramento, in the 1872 Crocker gallery building and the 125,000-square-foot Teel Family Pavilion (museum website, History page).

The collection began with Edwin and Margaret Crocker; Margaret gave the gallery building and collection to the City of Sacramento in 1885. The Teel Family Pavilion, designed by Gwathmey Siegel & Associates Architects, opened on 10 October 2010 (museum website, History page).

What is there: more than 32,000 works (museum website, About page). The founding collection included 701 paintings and 1,344 master drawings, plus works commissioned from California artists; Jennie Crocker Fassett later gave Korean ceramics, jade, ivory and sculpture. Areas include California art from the Gold Rush to the present, Modern and Contemporary, Native American, American, Ceramics, European, African, Glass, Enamels, Ancient Americas, Asian, Photography and Oceanic art (museum website).
funding_verdict: Crocker Art Museum: mainly private gifts, with a public-owned founding gift

name: Utah Museum of Fine Arts
overview: Art museum of the University of Utah in the Marcia and John Price Museum Building, 410 Campus Center Drive, between Rice-Eccles Stadium and the Jon M. Huntsman Center (museum website).

It traces its start to a small gallery opened in 1914 in the university's Park Building; after a gift of art from Winifred Kimball Hudnut it was incorporated as the Utah Museum of Fine Arts and reopened in 1951 (museum website).
It moved to the Arts and Architecture Center in 1970 and in 2001 to the 74,000 square foot Price Building, designed by Machado and Silvetti with Prescott Muir Architects (museum website).
funding_verdict: Utah Museum of Fine Arts: university and public money with private gifts, led by the Price family

name: Artpace San Antonio
overview: Non-profit contemporary art residency and exhibition space at 445 N Main Ave, downtown San Antonio (Artpace visit page).

Founded in 1993 by the artist, collector and businesswoman Linda Pace (1945 to 2007) and opened to the public in 1995. Robert Storr, then senior curator at the Museum of Modern Art, chose the inaugural artists (Artpace site). Wikipedia says she launched it through the Pace-Roberts Foundation for Contemporary Art, since renamed the Linda Pace Foundation.
The building is a former 1920s Hudson automobile dealership with 18,000 square feet, five exhibition spaces, an archives and research library, a workshop and event areas (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Artpace San Antonio: mainly private: the Linda Pace Foundation, with federal, state, city and foundation grants

name: San Antonio Museum of Art
overview: San Antonio Museum of Art, 200 West Jones Avenue, in the Lone Star Brewery building (museum website).
The site lists it as founded in 1981 (museum website).
The pages read gave no collection count or archive; a restaurant, shop, group tours and event rentals are offered.
funding_verdict: San Antonio Museum of Art: private contributions and endowment, funders not named in the pages read

name: Witte Museum
overview: Witte Museum, 3801 Broadway, San Antonio (museum website).

School teacher and botanist Ellen Schulz Quillin began working toward a museum in 1923; Alfred G. Witte left $65,000 for it when he died in 1925 and the City matched it. The museum opened on 8 October 1926 (museum website, History page).
What is there: about 320,000 artifacts and specimens stored at the B. Naylor Morton Research and Collections Center and an offsite repository (museum website).
funding_verdict: Witte Museum: private gifts and a capital campaign, with City of San Antonio operations support

name: Galería de la Raza
overview: Non-profit Xicane/Latine art space in San Francisco's Mission District, with two sites: Studio 24 at 2779 Folsom Street (education annex and offices) and Studio 16 at 2840 16th Street (main gallery and performance space, listed as under construction).

Founded in 1970 by Chicano artists and activists. It began in a storefront at 14th Street and Valencia, and in 1972 moved to 24th Street and Bryant (stated by the space). Wikipedia names Rupert García, Peter Rodríguez and Ralph Maradiaga among the founders.
Peter Rodríguez named the Galería (stated by the space). René Yañez became its first artistic director and Maradiaga its first administrative director (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Galería de la Raza: mainly donations and grants: a 501(c)(3) non-profit whose revenue is almost entirely contributions

name: Southern Exposure (SoEx)
overview: Artist-centred nonprofit gallery and arts organisation at 3030 20th Street in the Mission District of San Francisco, active in the Bay Area since 1974. Its mission covers artist-centred support, experimentation, education and public engagement (Southern Exposure).

Founded in 1974 at Project Artaud, San Francisco's oldest artist-owned live/work space, in a former American Can Company factory, as an artists' collective showing emerging artists as an alternative to commercial galleries (Southern Exposure history page).
Earlier name: the American Can Collective Gallery. After a lawsuit over the name it became Southern Exposure in February 1976 (Southern Exposure history page).
funding_verdict: Southern Exposure: mixed public and private: government arts grants, a Warhol Foundation partnership, an annual auction and individual donors

name: Museum of International Folk Art
overview: Museum of International Folk Art, 706 Camino Lejo, Museum Hill, Santa Fe; part of the New Mexico Department of Cultural Affairs (museum website).
The page says the Florence Dibell Bartlett Collection was donated by 'the founder' in the late 1940s; it does not state the opening year.
What is there: the Girard Collection, donated by Alexander and Susan Girard, shown in the Girard Wing; the page gives no object count (museum website).
funding_verdict: Museum of International Folk Art: state agency, with foundation grants and a friends group

name: Contemporary Art Museum St. Louis
overview: The Contemporary Art Museum St. Louis is at 3750 Washington Boulevard in the Grand Center Arts District in midtown St. Louis (museum website, plan your visit page).
The pages read do not give its founding date.

What is there: it has no permanent collection, which the museum says lets it respond to the art world and the local community; it shows contemporary work and runs more than 100 public programmes a year, most free (museum website, mission page).
funding_verdict: Contemporary Art Museum St. Louis: mainly private contributions, plus investment income, free to enter
